d:
The weight of the vehicle in kilograms.
  • Affects collision physics and suspension compression.

Aerodynamic drag coefficient.
  • Higher values slow the vehicle more at high speed.
  • This value controls how much air resistance the vehicle feels when moving fast. Think of it like how wind pushes against a car as it drives faster.
  • If the vehicle is too fast, raise the drag to slow it down.
  • If it’s too slow, lower the drag to let it go faster.

Scales the aerodynamic downforce applied to the car. This value controls how much extra force pushes the car down onto the road when it’s going fast. It helps the tires stick better to the road, especially at high speeds — just like real-life racecars that have big spoilers or wings.
  • Higher values increase grip at speed.
  • Try 10000 value to see the difference.

This value decides how deep the vehicle can go underwater before it starts to float temporarily (like a momentary bounce), before sinking for real.
  • 85.0 = 85% submerged to float.
  • 100.0: Has to be fully underwater before it floats — then sinks.
  • Invalid value (e.g., 2.0 or text): Car sinks instantly but the driver doesn’t drown. Vehicle may later teleport back to the surface weirdly.

This setting lets you move the car’s center of gravity (CoG) — basically, the balance point of the vehicle. Think of it like how a see-saw tips depending on where you place the weight.

Changing this affects how the car behaves when:

  • Turning
    • Will it roll or grip?
  • Jumping
    • Nose-heavy or tail-heavy?
  • Driving sideways or upside down
    • Will it spin or stay balanced?

Format: vecCentreOfMassOffset x="0.0" y="0.0" z="0.0"

  • X: left/right (− = left, + = right)
    • Shift weight side-to-side
    • Used to fix off-center balance (rarely changed)
  • Y: front/back (− = rear, + = front)
    • Makes the car nose-heavy or rear-heavy
  • Z: up/down (− = lower, + = higher)
    • Controls how high or low the balance is
    • This is the most important value!

This controls how much the vehicle resists rotating around each axis — in other words, how much it "fights back" against flipping, rolling, or spinning.

Think of it like adjusting how heavy or agile the car feels during:

  • Hard braking or acceleration (tilting forward/back)
  • Cornering (leaning side to side)
  • Steering (how fast the car turns or reacts to input)
  • Mid-air rotations (flips, spins)

Each axis affects different types of rotation:

  • X (Pitch - front/back tilt)
    • Controls how much the car tilts when braking or accelerating
    • Also affects how easily the car flips end-over-end in the air
    • Lower values = more tilt and easier flips
    • Higher values = more stable and less nose dive
  • Y (Roll - side-to-side lean)
    • Affects how much the vehicle leans during turns or in mid-air
    • Lower values = more body roll, more playful/loose
    • Higher values = stiffer turning and more stable
  • Z (Yaw - rotation/spin)
    • Controls how quickly the car rotates left/right when steering
    • Lower values = fast, arcade-like steering
    • Higher values = smoother, more realistic turning
    • Recommended to keep above 2.0 for natural behavior

Note: Some vehicles (like police3, Gang Burrito, 190Z, and Zion Classic) respond unusually to this setting — they rotate too slowly unless you lower the values.

Motorcycles ignore this setting completely.

Controls how the engine power is distributed between the front and rear wheels — essentially determining if the vehicle is rear-wheel drive (RWD), front-wheel drive (FWD), or all-wheel drive (AWD/4WD).

This directly affects how the car launches, handles corners, and loses/gains traction under throttle.

  • 0.0 — 100% Rear-Wheel Drive (RWD)
    • More oversteer and tail-happy behavior
    • Better for drifting or high-speed stability
    • Common in sports cars, muscle cars, supercars
  • 1.0 — 100% Front-Wheel Drive (FWD)
    • More understeer and nose-heavy handling
    • Good grip for everyday driving, poor for drifting
    • Used in most economy and compact cars
  • 0.01 to 0.99 — All-Wheel Drive / Four-Wheel Drive (AWD/4WD)
    • Power is split between front and rear axles
    • 0.5 = Perfect 50/50 split (true AWD)
    • Higher values (e.g., 0.7) = front-biased AWD
    • Lower values (e.g., 0.3) = rear-biased AWD
    • Great for off-roading, rally cars, or traction-heavy builds

Tip: Pair this setting with fInitialDriveForce and fTractionCurve* values to fine-tune handling behavior.

Sets the number of forward gears (transmission speeds) the vehicle has.

This value affects how the car accelerates and shifts through the gears during driving.

  • Minimum: 1 gear
  • Maximum (safe): 8 gears for stable shifting behavior
  • Maximum (supported): 10 gears starting from game version 1.0.1604.0 and above

Important Notes:

  • Using more than 8 gears can lead to gear ratio issues and downshifting bugs, especially if the top gear is 9 or higher.
  • Gear ratios beyond the 8th gear may overwrite unrelated data in the vehicle’s memory structure, leading to unpredictable behavior.
  • The final gear ratio is static and does not adjust based on gear count — meaning 6th or 7th gear might be taller (faster) than the final gear, causing awkward shifts.
  • For realistic or race-like behavior, 6–7 gears are generally optimal.

Recommended: Stay between 4 to 7 gears unless you know how to manually adjust gear ratios properly in the transmission data.

Controls the base engine torque applied to the wheels, directly influencing the vehicle’s acceleration. It is affected by the vehicle's weight.

Formula: fInitialDriveForce = TorqueWheelsNm / VehicleWeightKg

This means heavier vehicles require more drive force to accelerate at the same rate as lighter vehicles.

  • 0.01 – 0.40: Typical range for most vehicles
  • 1.0: Uses the calculated base drive force as-is (no scaling)
  • > 1.0: Increases acceleration significantly — use for high-performance or unrealistic setups
  • < 1.0: Decreases acceleration — good for trucks, buses, or realistic slow vehicles

Effect:

  • Higher values = faster acceleration, stronger launch
  • Lower values = slower, heavier-feeling car
  • This value is not the same as horsepower, but it heavily contributes to it
  • Best paired with correct values for fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel and fDriveBiasFront for realistic tuning

Tip: Start around 0.20–0.35 for most sedans or sports cars, and adjust based on feel. Test in-game with different vehicle weights for accurate results.

Controls how quickly the engine RPM (revolutions per minute) can increase or decrease — essentially simulating the "rotational momentum" of the drivetrain.

Think of it like: a lighter flywheel = faster engine revs (high inertia value), a heavier flywheel = slower revs (low inertia value).

Effects:

  • Higher values = faster RPM increase (engine revs up quickly)
  • Lower values = slower RPM change (engine takes longer to reach redline)
  • This affects how fast the engine responds to throttle input, not the actual vehicle acceleration
  • Too low (e.g., < 0.5) can negatively affect performance in high-acceleration vehicles

Value range:

  • 0.01 – 0.50: Slow-revving engines (trucks, heavy vehicles, realism)
  • 0.50 – 1.0: Normal range (most standard vehicles)
  • 1.0: Default — no RPM response modification
  • 1.0 – 2.0+: Fast-revving engines (sports cars, race cars, tuned engines)

Tip: Combine this setting with fInitialDriveForce and fClutchChangeRate* values to tune responsiveness and shifting behavior.

Controls how fast the clutch engages during an upshift (shifting to a higher gear while accelerating). This affects how quickly the vehicle transitions between gears under throttle.

Higher values = faster shifts, with less time lost between gears. Lower values = slower, more realistic or smoother shifts.

Value guidelines:

  • 1.0 = Approx. 0.9 seconds per upshift (realistic for regular vehicles)
  • 4.0 – 7.0 = Snappy shifting (sports cars, tuned cars)
  • 8.0 – 13.0 = Very quick gear changes (race cars, arcade feel)
  • Above 13.0 = Not recommended — may cause bugs or unrealistic shift behavior

Tips:

  • Use higher values for race or performance vehicles to reduce gear lag
  • Use lower values for trucks, old/classic cars, or to simulate automatic transmissions
  • Pair with fClutchChangeRateScaleDownShift for balanced shifting

Controls how quickly the clutch engages when downshifting (shifting to a lower gear). This affects how fast the vehicle can drop gears, especially under braking or engine braking conditions.

Higher values = quicker downshifts, which means faster throttle response when dropping gears. Lower values = slower, smoother, or more realistic downshifting.

Value guidelines:

  • 1.0 = Approx. 0.9 seconds per downshift (default baseline)
  • 4.0 – 7.0 = Fast and responsive downshifts (ideal for sports and performance cars)
  • 8.0 – 13.0 = Ultra-fast shifting (race cars or arcade-style handling)
  • Above 13.0 = Not recommended — may cause glitches or shifting instability

Notes:

  • This setting does not directly affect engine braking strength, but it impacts how fast the lower gear is engaged
  • Recommended to pair with fClutchChangeRateScaleUpShift for consistent transmission behavior
  • Lower values (1.0–2.5) can simulate slower manual or automatic gearboxes

Sets the vehicle’s theoretical maximum speed at redline in top gear on flat terrain. This effectively adjusts the final drive ratio of the transmission, influencing how long each gear is.

Important: This value does not guarantee the vehicle will reach this speed — acceleration, drag, and other factors like fInitialDriveForce and fInitialDragCoeff still apply.

Speed Conversion:

  • fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel * 0.82 ≈ speed in mph
  • fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel * 1.32 ≈ speed in km/h
  • To get fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel from km/h: km/h * 0.75
  • To get fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel from mph: mph * 1.22

Gear Ratio Formula:

  • TopSpeedKph = (fInitialDriveMaxFlatVel * 1.2) / GearRatio
  • Default GTA top gear ratio is 0.9
  • To calculate for a specific gear, replace 0.9 with that gear’s ratio

Value Range: 0.00 – 500.0+

Tuning Tips:

  • Use higher values to simulate longer gearing and higher top speed potential
  • Use lower values to shorten gear length, improve acceleration (especially in lower-powered cars)
  • Best used in combination with nInitialDriveGears and fInitialDriveForce for balanced results
  • Overly high values can make gears feel “flat” and reduce acceleration in all gears

Controls how strong the vehicle’s brakes are by multiplying the base deceleration calculated by the game. Affects how quickly the vehicle slows down when braking.

Higher values = stronger braking, while lower values = longer stopping distances.

Value range:

  • 0.01 – 0.50: Weak brakes — used for heavy vehicles, realism, or slippery surfaces
  • 0.50 – 1.0: Standard range — realistic braking for normal cars
  • 1.0: Default — uses the game’s calculated braking force without adjustment
  • 1.0 – 2.0+: Very strong brakes — great for sports, race, or arcade-style vehicles

Important: Increasing fBrakeForce beyond a certain point will not increase stopping power if the wheels are already limited by traction.

Traction interaction:

  • To ensure full braking potential is used, set:
  • fBrakeForce > fTractionCurveMax / 4 (tested mainly on cars)
  • Otherwise, the brakes may lock up or lose grip before reaching full deceleration

Tips:

  • Pair with fHandBrakeForce for balanced tuning
  • Too high of a value may cause vehicles to skid or stop unrealistically fast
  • Test braking under different speeds and surfaces to tune for realism

Determines how braking force is distributed between the front and rear axles.

Value Range:

  • 0.0 = 100% rear brake force
  • 0.5 = Equal braking force on front and rear axles (50/50)
  • 1.0 = 100% front brake force

How it works:

  • Values between 0.01 – 0.49 = rear-biased braking
  • Values between 0.51 – 0.99 = front-biased braking
  • Typical real-world vehicles use around 0.60 – 0.70 for better braking stability (more braking force at the front due to weight transfer)

Things to keep in mind:

  • A higher front bias (> 0.5) does not always mean the front wheels will lock or trigger ABS before the rear
  • ABS lock behavior depends on additional vehicle flags (see strModelFlags for advanced tuning)
  • Too much rear brake bias can make the car unstable under heavy braking and increase spin risk

Recommended Setup:

  • 0.60 – 0.70 for most sedans, sports cars, and realistic setups
  • 0.50 for balanced or AWD vehicles
  • < 0.50 only for drift or stunt vehicles where rear bias is desired

Controls how strong the handbrake (usually bound to spacebar or controller trigger) applies braking force to the rear wheels.

Used primarily for drifting, sliding, or locking the rear wheels during cornering or stunts.

Higher values = stronger rear wheel lock-up. Lower values = softer, more gradual slide.

Typical Value Ranges:

  • 0.3 – 0.6: Light/moderate handbrake (street cars, AWD vehicles)
  • 0.7 – 1.0: Aggressive lock-up (sport/rally cars)
  • 1.0 – 2.0+: Extreme locking force (drift builds, arcade behavior)

Notes:

  • Only affects rear wheels — front wheels are unaffected
  • Best paired with tuned fBrakeBiasFront and fTractionCurve* values for proper drift behavior
  • Too high of a value may cause vehicles to spin or lose control easily

Defines the maximum steering angle (in degrees) the front wheels can turn.

A higher value allows for tighter low-speed turning (smaller turning radius), while a lower value limits steering angle for stability at higher speeds.

Typical Range:

  • 30 – 45: Normal for most street and sports cars
  • 50 – 60: Suitable for drift cars or tight maneuvering vehicles
  • 60 – 90: Extreme steering angle (use with caution)

Steering Behavior:

  • At high speed, GTA V applies steering assist, reducing the steering angle proportionally based on fSteeringLock
  • Too low = car becomes unresponsive at speed
  • Too high = car may oversteer or push front tires into understeer/skid

Tuning Tip: For optimal grip and control, align fSteeringLock with fTractionCurveLateral.

Recommended formula:

fSteeringLock = (fTractionCurveLateral * 1.25) + 10

Example: If fTractionCurveLateral is 22.5, then a good fSteeringLock would be around 38.

Default: Many GTA V vehicles use 40.0 as a balanced value.

Defines the maximum lateral grip (cornering force) the tires can produce before beginning to lose traction.

This is the peak value in the tire grip curve — essentially the point where the tires have the most control during cornering or acceleration before sliding starts.

Higher values = more grip during high-speed turns and sudden direction changes.

Typical Range:

  • 1.0 – 2.0: Slippery vehicles or poor tires (off-road, snow, worn tires)
  • 2.0 – 2.5: Standard road cars
  • 2.5 – 3.5: Sports and performance vehicles
  • 3.5 – 5.0+: Racing tires, high-grip or arcade-style behavior

Important: This value is closely tied to fSteeringLock. If fTractionCurveMax is too high without enough steering lock, the vehicle won’t turn sharply enough. If it's too low with too much steering, the car will lose grip easily.

Related Tuning Tips:

  • Pair with fTractionCurveMin to define grip during sliding or at high slip angles
  • Use with fLowSpeedTractionLossMult to balance low-speed control
  • Recommended fSteeringLock formula: (fTractionCurveMax * 1.25) + 10

Controls the tire grip during sliding or loss-of-traction situations — such as wheel spin, drifting, oversteer, or understeer.

This value represents the minimum lateral grip after the vehicle exceeds the peak grip defined by fTractionCurveMax.

Lower values = more sliding (useful for drift cars), while higher values maintain control during slip.

Typical Range:

  • 0.5 – 1.5: Drift or stunt vehicles (easier to lose grip)
  • 1.5 – 2.0: Standard cars with balanced slip behavior
  • 2.0 – 3.0: High-grip race or performance vehicles

Tuning Tips:

  • Should generally be lower than fTractionCurveMax
  • Set a bigger gap between Max and Min for easier drifting (e.g., Max 3.0 / Min 1.0)
  • Smaller gap = more grip retention during aggressive driving (e.g., Max 2.8 / Min 2.5)
  • Use together with fTractionCurveLateral for full control of grip response

Real-World Analogy: This is how much grip the tires still provide after you’ve pushed them too far — like sliding through a turn or spinning out under throttle.

Defines the shape and peak position of the tire's lateral traction curve, often referred to as the "slip angle" — the angle at which tires produce peak cornering grip.

This value determines how responsive or forgiving the vehicle is to quick steering and high-speed cornering:

  • Lower values: Quick grip response, sharp handling — but more likely to lose traction if pushed too far (less forgiving)
  • Higher values: Slower steering response, but smoother and more stable grip transition (more forgiving)

Slip Angle Estimate: The actual peak grip angle is calculated as:
fTractionCurveLateral / 2 (in degrees)

Typical Range:

  • 16 – 22: High-performance or race cars (fast response)
  • 22 – 28: Standard road cars (balanced behavior)
  • 28 – 34+: Heavier or more stable vehicles (trucks, off-road)

Related Tuning Tips:

  • This value pairs directly with fSteeringLock to ensure steering input matches optimal tire angle
  • Recommended formula: fSteeringLock = (fTractionCurveLateral * 1.25) + 10
  • Too low = snappy but twitchy grip; too high = sluggish steering response

Summary: Use this to balance how fast and how safely your vehicle responds to quick direction changes and cornering forces.

Controls the maximum lateral sidewall travel (in meters) before traction loss begins to stabilize. This simulates how much the tire can flex sideways during cornering or sliding before it pulls back.

Unit: meters of lateral sidewall flex (tire "squish")

This setting adds a dynamic force that helps the car return to stability after a slide. The larger the delta, the more noticeable the vehicle will "snap back" into alignment after drifting or rapid turning.

Behavior:

  • Higher values = more noticeable rebound or pull-in effect after a slide
  • Lower values = less stabilization, more floaty or loose drift behavior

Common Use: Used to fine-tune post-slide control or responsiveness mid-corner. Particularly noticeable during transitions (drift → grip).

Typical Range: 0.01 – 0.15

Tuning Tip: Increase this value slightly if you want the vehicle to naturally realign itself faster after skidding or drifting.

Summary: Simulates tire deformation under lateral load. Affects how strongly the car “snaps” back into control during or after a corner or slide.

Controls how much traction is artificially reduced at low speeds. This primarily affects wheelspin when accelerating from a stop or during burnouts.

Higher values = more burnout and sliding at low speed, especially when pressing the throttle aggressively.

Lower values = better grip from a standstill, reducing tire spin and making launches more stable.

Typical Effects:

  • 0.0: No artificial traction loss — full grip at low speed
  • 0.5 – 1.0: Mild-to-moderate wheelspin (default balance)
  • 1.5 – 3.0+: Heavy burnouts, high tire spin on launch

Use Cases:

  • Set low for race cars, AWD, or realistic street driving
  • Set high for muscle cars, drag builds, or arcade-style launches

Note: This is a completely artificial value — it doesn’t simulate real physics, but rather adds or removes tire spin behavior under low-speed conditions.

Default: Most GTA V vehicles use 1.0.

Controls how much the vehicle is influenced by camber forces — primarily how much the suspension "leans" or rolls into corners due to road tilt or body roll.

This affects how strongly the vehicle is pushed in the direction of its body roll. It also accounts for the road’s camber (sideways slope).

Behavior:

  • Higher values (closer to 1.0): More roll stiffness and force toward the inside of the turn
  • Lower values (closer to 0.0): Weaker camber response, more natural suspension lean

Safe Range: 0.0 – 1.0
Warning: Values below 0.0 or above 1.0 can cause unstable or unrealistic physics behavior

Use Cases:

  • Set closer to 0.5 – 0.7 for most normal cars with balanced roll stiffness
  • Use 0.8+ for racing cars or go-karts that require strong force against roll
  • Use 0.2 – 0.4 for soft suspension vehicles like SUVs or off-roaders

Tip: Combine with fSuspensionForce and fAntiRollBarForce to fine-tune the vehicle’s handling balance during turns.

Defines how grip (traction) is distributed between the front and rear wheels.

Value Range: 0.01 – 0.99

  • 0.01: Rear axle gets all the grip (RWD behavior)
  • 0.99: Front axle gets all the grip (FWD behavior)
  • 0.50: Equal traction front and rear (balanced AWD/4WD)

Important:

  • 0.00 or 1.00: Invalid — causes tire physics to break (wheels won’t spawn or act properly)
  • Outside valid range: Vehicle will behave irrationally when touching the ground (floating, stuttering, or no control)

Use Cases:

  • Rear-biased (0.30 – 0.45): Drifting, RWD handling feel
  • Front-biased (0.55 – 0.70): Stable cornering and safer understeer
  • Balanced (≈ 0.50): True AWD / performance traction

Tuning Tip: Adjust this value together with fDriveBiasFront and fTractionCurveMin for refined acceleration and cornering behavior.

Summary: This setting doesn’t control how power is delivered (like fDriveBiasFront), but how much grip each axle gets when driving and cornering.

Adjusts how much traction (grip) is affected by surface material types — like asphalt, gravel, dirt, or mud.

Higher values: Amplify the effect of slippery surfaces, making the car more prone to sliding or losing control.

Lower values: Reduce the difference between road materials — making the car more stable across all terrain types.

Typical Value Range:

  • 0.5 – 0.9: Off-road stability (more consistent grip)
  • 1.0 (default): Normal road behavior (standard material grip effects)
  • 1.2 – 2.0: Slippery handling, more realistic surface-based sliding (use for drifting or unpredictable terrain)

Use Cases:

  • Set lower for rally cars or vehicles that need grip on mixed surfaces
  • Set higher for arcade-style sliding, stunt cars, or vehicles meant to feel light and loose

Tip: Pairs well with fTractionCurveMin and fLowSpeedTractionLossMult to control overall grip behavior across speed and terrain.

Summary: This value multiplies how strongly the road surface material affects your grip. Lower = more stable, higher = more slide.

Controls the stiffness of the suspension springs. This determines how strongly the vehicle resists compression and extension (bouncing up and down).

Higher values: Stiffer suspension — less bounce, better stability, but less comfort

Lower values: Softer suspension — more bounce and body movement, but better absorption over bumps

Technical Formula: 1 / (Force * NumWheels) = suspension travel (how much suspension can move)

Typical Range: 1.0 – 10.0

Behavior:

  • Set higher for race cars, sports cars, or vehicles that flip too easily
  • Set lower for off-road vehicles, trucks, or soft suspension setups

Tip: If your car feels floaty or bounces a lot when turning, increase this value.
Combine with fSuspensionCompDamp and fSuspensionReboundDamp for fine control over suspension behavior.

Summary: Controls how hard the vehicle springs push back when compressed. Affects ride comfort, cornering stability, and bouncing.

Controls how much the suspension resists when it compresses — such as when landing, braking, or hitting a bump.

Higher values: Stiffer compression — suspension compresses slower, reducing bounce and dive

Lower values: Softer compression — more body movement and smoother landings, but can feel floaty

Behavior:

  • High damping helps reduce bouncing and keeps the car more planted
  • Low damping allows more movement — useful for off-road or soft setups

Typical Range: 0.5 – 4.0

Use Cases:

  • 2.0 – 3.5: Race cars and sports cars for better control and less dive
  • 1.0 – 2.0: Balanced street vehicles
  • 0.5 – 1.5: Off-road or comfort-oriented vehicles

Tip: Tune alongside fSuspensionReboundDamp and fSuspensionForce to achieve the right handling feel.
Too high a value may make the car feel stiff or skittish over uneven surfaces.

Summary: Compression damping affects how quickly the suspension squishes down under pressure — like from bumps or weight shifts.

Controls how much the suspension resists when it extends back after being compressed — such as after a bump, landing, or weight transfer.

Higher values: Slower rebound — suspension takes longer to return to full height, creating a more planted and stable feel

Lower values: Faster rebound — suspension returns quickly, but may feel bouncy or unstable

Behavior:

  • Too low = bouncy or floaty ride (especially after bumps or jumps)
  • Too high = suspension feels stuck or slow to reset after compression

Typical Range: 0.5 – 4.0

Use Cases:

  • 2.0 – 3.5: Track or high-performance vehicles for tight, stable rebound
  • 1.0 – 2.0: Street vehicles for balanced ride quality
  • 0.5 – 1.5: Off-road or soft suspension for quicker recovery over uneven terrain

Tip: Rebound damping works with fSuspensionCompDamp to shape how the suspension reacts to movement. Rebound should generally be slightly stronger than compression for stable handling.

Summary: This setting manages how quickly the suspension returns to its original position after compressing — directly affecting stability, cornering response, and post-jump behavior.

Sets how far the wheels can move upward (compress) from their resting position — measured in meters.

Higher values: Allows more upward travel — softer feel, better for off-road or bumpy terrain

Lower values: Limits compression travel — stiffer ride, better for low-profile or track vehicles

Value Range: Typically -0.1 to 0.5

Note: This is a positive upward offset in the vehicle model’s local axis. Negative values are rare and may cause visual bugs.

Behavior:

  • Impacts how much the suspension can absorb bumps and weight shifts
  • If too small, suspension may bottom out or feel rigid
  • If too large, wheels may clip into the fenders or body

Tip: Use together with fSuspensionLowerLimit to set total travel distance.
For off-road or lifted vehicles, increase both upper and lower limits.

Summary: Controls how far the wheels can move upward into the wheel arch during suspension compression.

Sets how far the wheels can move downward (extend) from their original position — measured in meters.

Higher (more negative) values: More suspension droop — useful for off-road, rally, or vehicles needing extended wheel travel

Lower (less negative) values: Less downward movement — tighter suspension feel for racing or lowered vehicles

Typical Range: -0.01 to -0.25

Behavior:

  • Too small (near 0) = suspension feels stiff and limited
  • Too large (very negative) = vehicle may sag, bounce, or float excessively

Tip: This value is almost always negative and defines how far wheels can "drop" below the chassis. Works together with fSuspensionUpperLimit to define total suspension travel.

Use Cases:

  • -0.1 to -0.2: Normal street vehicles
  • -0.2 to -0.4: Off-road or rally setups
  • -0.05 or less: Stiff sports/race setups with minimal droop

Summary: Controls how far the suspension can stretch downward — key for determining grip and stability over uneven terrain.

Adjusts the vertical position of the vehicle's body relative to its wheels — effectively raising or lowering the ride height visually, without changing actual suspension travel.

Positive values: Raise the vehicle body — creates a lifted look (may expose suspension gaps)

Negative values: Lower the vehicle body — lowers stance, ideal for sport/street aesthetics

Typical Range: -0.10 to +0.10
Fine adjustments often use -0.01 to +0.01

Behavior:

  • Does not affect suspension strength or travel directly
  • Only changes how high or low the body sits on the wheels
  • Too low: wheels may clip through fenders or float off suspension arms
  • Too high: visible gap between wheels and body or disconnected-looking suspension

Use Cases:

  • −0.02 to −0.04: Lowered stance for race cars or street tuners
  • 0.00: Default, neutral ride height
  • +0.02 or more: Off-road, lifted trucks, or monster builds

Tip: This value should be adjusted in small steps (0.01–0.02) unless the model allows more room. Large changes can cause visual glitches.

Summary: Raises or lowers the vehicle’s body relative to the wheels, mostly for visual stance — does not affect performance unless extreme.

Adjusts the distribution of suspension stiffness between the front and rear wheels — useful for balancing the vehicle when there’s uneven weight or different axle loads.

Value Range: 0.0 to 1.0

  • 0.5: Equal suspension strength front and rear (default for balanced vehicles)
  • > 0.5: Front suspension is stiffer — ideal for front-heavy vehicles or trucks with lighter rear ends
  • < 0.5: Rear suspension is stiffer — good for rear-engine or rear-heavy vehicles

Behavior:

  • Influences how the car reacts during braking, acceleration, and over bumps
  • Too much front bias = rear feels soft or unstable under load
  • Too much rear bias = front may dive too much during braking

Use Cases:

  • 0.55 – 0.65: Pickup trucks or front-heavy vehicles
  • 0.45 – 0.50: Rear-heavy cars or balanced performance setups

Tip: Match this setting with your vehicle’s weight distribution and number of wheels per axle. For example, trucks with multiple rear wheels often need stronger front suspension bias.

Summary: Controls which end of the vehicle has stronger suspension support — affects body movement, weight transfer, and cornering stability.

Controls how much force is transferred from one wheel to the opposite wheel when the suspension compresses — simulating the effect of anti-roll (sway) bars.

Higher values: Less body roll during turns, stiffer lateral stability

Lower values: More body roll, softer feel — better for off-road or uneven terrain

Typical Range: 0.0 to 1.5 (default ~0.5)

Behavior:

  • Reduces lean when cornering
  • Improves stability in high-speed turns
  • Too high = overly stiff, possible loss of grip on uneven roads
  • Too low = excessive body roll, slower handling response

Use Cases:

  • 0.4 – 0.7: Balanced street and sport vehicles
  • 0.8 – 1.2: High-performance or race cars
  • 0.0 – 0.3: Off-road or rock-crawling vehicles (to allow articulation)

Tip: Use in combination with fAntiRollBarBiasFront to adjust how this stiffness is distributed between the front and rear axles.

Summary: Controls body roll resistance during cornering — higher values = flatter turns and tighter handling.

Distributes the anti-roll bar (sway bar) force between the front and rear axles. This determines which end of the vehicle resists body roll more during cornering.

Value Range: 0.0 to 1.0

  • 0.0: 100% rear anti-roll force — rear is stiff, front is loose
  • 0.5: 50/50 split — balanced roll resistance front and rear
  • 1.0: 100% front anti-roll force — front is stiff, rear is loose

Behavior:

  • More front bias (e.g. 0.6 – 0.8): Reduces front body roll, increases understeer
  • More rear bias (e.g. 0.2 – 0.4): Reduces rear body roll, increases oversteer
  • Neutral (0.5): Balanced — good for general road use

Use Cases:

  • Sports cars: ~0.55 to 0.65 (slight front bias for stability)
  • Drift cars: ~0.4 or lower (more rear stiffness = easier to swing out)
  • Off-road: ~0.5 or lower (for more articulation)

Tip: Use together with fAntiRollBarForce to control overall stiffness, then fine-tune the balance using this value.

Summary: Controls how the anti-roll force is split between front and rear — affects understeer vs oversteer behavior in corners.

Sets the height of the roll center for the front axle, measured from the base of the vehicle model (ground level), in meters. The roll center is a pivot point around which the vehicle rolls (leans) during cornering.

How It Works:

  • Higher values: Less body roll — front suspension resists leaning
  • Lower values: More body roll — front suspension leans more in turns

Behavior:

  • If the roll center is too high (above the center of mass), it can cause unnatural handling like the “Tyrus effect” — where the car leans inward (negative roll)
  • If it’s too low (far below the center of mass), the vehicle may roll too much and become unstable or prone to rollover

Suggested Values:

  • 0.20 – 0.45: Typical for most vehicles
  • 0.50+: Use with caution — only if center of mass is very low
  • < 0.15: Can cause excessive roll or instability

Tip: Match this value with your center of mass height (vecCentreOfMassOffset.z) to control lean without causing weird behavior. Use together with fRollCentreHeightRear to fine-tune front/rear roll balance.

Summary: Adjusts how much the front of the vehicle leans in corners. Higher = flatter handling, lower = more dramatic roll and weight shift.

Sets the roll center height for the rear axle — the point around which the rear end of the vehicle rolls during cornering. Measured in meters from the bottom of the vehicle model (road level).

How It Works:

  • Higher values: Less rear body roll — tighter, flatter rear-end behavior
  • Lower values: More rear body roll — greater rear-end lean and weight shift

Important Dynamics:

  • Raising the rear roll center relative to the front shifts more cornering load to the front, helping reduce understeer
  • Lowering the rear roll center makes the rear roll more — potentially increasing understeer or allowing for drift-style oversteer depending on grip balance
  • If the roll center is set above the vehicle’s center of mass, it can cause “negative roll” or odd leaning behavior (known as the “Tyrus Effect”)

Suggested Ranges:

  • 0.25 – 0.50: Balanced street or track cars
  • Above 0.50: Use cautiously — only when center of mass is very low
  • Below 0.20: Can cause excessive rear-end roll and instability

Tips:

  • Use in combination with fRollCentreHeightFront to fine-tune cornering behavior
  • More rear roll center height than front: Increases turn-in response
  • More front roll center height than rear: Increases corner stability

Summary: Controls how much the rear of the car leans in turns. Helps tune understeer/oversteer balance and body control during cornering.

Controls how much physical damage the vehicle takes from impacts such as crashes, bumps, and landings. This value multiplies the base damage the game applies when the vehicle collides with anything.

What It Affects:

  • Body deformation (dents, crumples, parts falling off)
  • Engine damage (can lead to smoke/fire/stall)
  • Wheels or gas tank catching fire after severe impact

Value Range:

  • 0.0: No collision damage at all (invincible car body and engine)
  • 1.0: Normal GTA V collision damage
  • 10.0: Ten times more damage from every crash

Use Cases:

  • Low values (0.1–0.4): Useful for durable vehicles like off-roaders or armored cars
  • High values (2.0+): Good for fragile sports cars or hardcore realism
  • 0.0: Makes the vehicle immune to crash damage (but may still explode from bullets or fire)

Note: This value also affects whether the engine is damaged from impacts. Setting it to 0 disables engine failure from collisions.

Summary: Multiplier for all collision-based damage to the vehicle body, engine, and more.

Multiplies how much damage the vehicle takes from weapons, including bullets, explosions, and melee attacks. This value adjusts how vulnerable the vehicle is to combat-related threats.

What It Affects:

  • Bullet damage to body panels, windows, and tires
  • Explosive damage from grenades, RPGs, sticky bombs, etc.
  • Firearms causing engine failure or vehicle ignition

Value Range:

  • 0.0: Vehicle is immune to all weapon damage
  • 1.0: Default GTA V weapon damage
  • 10.0: Takes ten times more damage from all weapons

Use Cases:

  • 0.0: Use for unbreakable props or cinematic-only vehicles
  • 0.1 – 0.4: Makes vehicles more resistant to damage, like armored cars
  • 2.0+: Increases realism or fragility for custom gameplay modes

Note: This does not affect how weapons interact with pedestrians or environment — only vehicles.

Summary: Controls how easily the vehicle takes damage from bullets, explosives, and other weapons.

Controls how much the vehicle's body visually crumples or bends when damaged. This affects the visual deformation — like dents, twisted frames, or panels bending — but not actual engine or performance damage.

What It Affects:

  • Visible body deformation from crashes or hard impacts
  • Crushed hoods, doors, bumpers, fenders, etc.
  • Severity of model distortion (especially for cinematic or crash-test builds)

Value Range:

  • 0.0: Vehicle body will not visually deform, regardless of impact force
  • 1.0: Standard GTA V deformation
  • 10.0: Extreme deformation — even small hits may crush panels significantly

Use Cases:

  • 0.0 – 0.2: Use for strong/rigid vehicles like trucks or armored vehicles
  • 1.0: Balanced realism for regular cars
  • 3.0+: Great for cinematic destruction, soft vehicles, or demolition derby setups

Note: This is purely visual — it doesn’t affect drivability or engine performance unless combined with other damage multipliers.

Summary: Scales how much the car visually deforms when damaged. Higher = more crumpling.

Controls how much damage the vehicle's engine takes from collisions or attacks. A higher value makes the engine more fragile and more likely to fail or catch fire. This affects gameplay performance — engine health, stalling, and explosions.

What It Affects:

  • Engine health loss during impacts or crashes
  • Increased chance of engine stalling or failing
  • Engine fires and explosions when severely damaged

Value Range:

  • 0.0: Engine is indestructible — no damage or failure
  • 1.0: Standard engine damage calculation
  • 10.0: Extremely fragile engine — small hits may destroy it

Use Cases:

  • 0.0 – 0.2: Ideal for armored or mission-critical vehicles
  • 0.5 – 1.0: Balanced setting for realism
  • 2.0+: For hardcore or cinematic setups where engine failure is common

Note: Engine damage is most sensitive to direct hood impacts, especially on low vehicles. Tall vehicles may absorb more front-end impact without triggering engine loss.

Summary: Multiplies how fast the engine breaks down from crashes or hits. Higher = more engine damage.

Defines the size of the vehicle's fuel tank in liters. Affects how much fuel leaks when the tank is punctured and is also used by certain fuel-consumption or refueling scripts.

What It Affects:

  • Amount of fuel that leaks when the gas tank is shot or damaged
  • Integration with custom fuel systems (like LegacyFuel or other mods)
  • May influence fire/explosion timing if fuel leaks and ignites

Value Range: Any realistic value in liters (e.g., 40.0 – 120.0)

Use Cases:

  • Motorcycles: ~15.0 – 20.0 L
  • Sports Cars: ~50.0 – 70.0 L
  • Trucks or SUVs: ~80.0 – 120.0 L

Note: This value has no effect unless fuel-related logic (like damage, fire, or scripting) references it.

Summary: Sets how much fuel the vehicle holds. Impacts leaks and fuel-based mods.

Sets the total engine oil capacity in liters. This value influences how long the engine can operate while leaking oil — usually after major damage. Once oil depletes, the engine starts emitting black smoke and eventually fails.

What It Affects:

  • How long the engine can run after taking oil-related damage
  • Length of time black smoke appears before engine shutdown
  • Used by some mods to simulate oil pressure/failure

Value Range: Typically between 2.0 and 12.0 liters

Use Cases:

  • Motorcycles: ~2.0 – 3.0 L
  • Sports/Regular Cars: ~4.0 – 6.0 L
  • Trucks or High-Performance Engines: ~8.0 – 12.0 L

Note: This value does not directly affect performance unless paired with scripts or damage behavior. However, black smoke and engine failure timing is indirectly influenced by it.

Summary: Sets how much engine oil is available. Affects how long the engine lasts after damage before it dies.

Sets how far the seat is positioned sideways (left or right) relative to the vehicle’s center. This is most noticeable when entering or exiting the vehicle — it adjusts how far the character shifts toward the door.

What It Affects:

  • Driver/passenger seating alignment with the vehicle door
  • Character entry/exit animations and positioning
  • Vehicle mod visuals and realism (e.g. when using custom models)

Value Range: Typically small values around -0.3 to +0.3

Interpretation:

  • Negative (-): Moves the seat left (toward the driver side)
  • Positive (+): Moves the seat right (toward the passenger side)

Example: Driver seat might use -0.25, passenger seat might use +0.25

Note: This has no impact on vehicle handling — it’s purely visual and positional.

Summary: Controls how far the seat is placed side-to-side inside the vehicle cabin.

Sets how far the seat is positioned forward or backward inside the vehicle (along the Y axis). It adjusts whether the seat is closer to the front or rear of the vehicle.

What It Affects:

  • How far the character sits toward the dashboard or the backrest
  • Interior alignment — useful for tuning modded or custom vehicles
  • Ensures animation and seating look realistic

Value Range: Usually from -1.0 (rear) to +1.0 (front)

Interpretation:

  • Negative (-): Moves the seat closer to the trunk/rear
  • Positive (+): Moves the seat closer to the hood/dashboard

Example: Rear seats may use -0.5, front seats may use +0.3

Note: This is a cosmetic positioning value, not related to handling or physics.

Summary: Controls front/back placement of the seat within the car's interior.

Sets how high or low the seat is placed in the vehicle (along the Z axis). This determines how far the character sits from the vehicle's floor or roof.

What It Affects:

  • How high the driver or passenger sits inside the vehicle
  • Visual alignment with steering wheels, dashboards, and windows
  • Can help fix clipping issues in custom vehicles

Value Range: Typically from -1.0 (lower/closer to the floor) to +1.0 (higher/closer to the roof)

Interpretation:

  • Negative (-): Lowers the seat toward the undercarriage
  • Positive (+): Raises the seat toward the roof

Example: Sports cars may use lower values like -0.3, while vans may use higher values like +0.2

Note: This only affects seating position and visuals — it has no impact on handling or physics.

Summary: Controls the vertical (up/down) placement of the seat inside the vehicle.

Represents the in-game value (worth) of the vehicle in dollars. This is used by various game mechanics and scripts.

What It Affects:

  • Vehicle resale or insurance cost (in some game modes)
  • Value displayed in vehicle shops or export missions
  • Economy-based systems in roleplay or custom servers

Value Range: Any positive integer. Typically from 500 to 2,000,000 depending on vehicle type.

Notes:

  • This value has no effect on performance or physics.
  • Useful for sorting vehicle classes (e.g., economy, sports, supercars).
  • Some modded shop or garage systems may use this to determine cost.

Summary: Sets how much the vehicle is worth in in-game currency.
